newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: East Europe mkts mixed, investors turn to Prague.
newsitem.headline: East Europe mkts mixed, investors turn to Prague.

text.p: Markets across central and eastern Europe were mixed this week, with key foreign investors turning their attention to Czech shares after recent strong gains in Hungary and Poland.
Bourses in Prague, Warsaw and Bratislava all gained ground, while Budapest dropped sharply on disappointing earnings reports and Croation shares eased. Romanian shares were mixed.
PRAGUE
Czech blue-chip shares surged early in the week, as a spate of buying from abroad helped buoy a market which was otherwise quiet.

Some analysts suggested that foreign investors may have decided to firm up their positions in the Czech Republic on the grounds that after strong gains in recent years in Poland and Hungary Prague was bound to be next.
"Fundamentally there's really no optimism...but after Hungary and Poland...some really believe that now is the timE to go long into Czech paper," said Radim Bajgar of ING Barings.
Profit-taking affected some of the major issues later in the week but the PX50 index still closed up one percent from Monday's open.
WARSAW

Polish shares rose one percent to 16,920.4 points this week and analysts said that despite another likely profit-taking fall on Monday, enough stocks were attractively priced to return to growth by the middle of next week.
They said gains should not prove as large as during the recent six-session 14.5-percent surge led by large-cap banks but that rises by industrials could lead to slower growth.

"Firms in the construction, power and furniture industries hich are gaining from the recent flooding are a lot cheaper than comparable firms in Hungary or Russia," said Dariusz Piszczatowski of Polish Development Bank (PBR) house.
The bourse was closed on Friday for the Assumption holiday.
BUDAPEST

The Budapest bourse's fortunes turned sharply this week with the market sliding over seven percent in the first four days of the week, including an almost six percent plunge on Monday, as some of the first half earnings reports caused disappointment among investors.
On Friday the bourse closed on a slightly positive note, but traders said the market was seeking direction after this week's hectic moves.

"Some decisive questions have to be answered in the next few days before the market begins to move," said Gyorgy Czipo of ING Barings. "Question remains where the dollar fixes, what steps the Fed will take and how investors react to earnings."
BRATISLAVA
The Bratislava Stock Exchange continued to suffer from the quiet summer season this week, though slightly more action was seen on the part of foreign players.

"Most of the trading, for what it is, is from abroad because local players see more profits in the current domestic money market where rates are hovering at around 20 percent," Peter Krutil of Creditanstalt said.
"I don't remember such a dull period," Kruilt said, adding he saw no light at then end of the tunnel yet.
BUCHAREST
Bucharest stocks traded mixed this week in thin demand due to the summer lull, traders said.
On Friday investor interest picked up in chemicals and pharmaceuticals, helping the Bucharest bourse to close slightly up, despite thin trading.

First-tier stars, chemical plant Oltchim firmed 200 lei to 4,150, while pharmaceuticals maker Antibiotice went up 300 lei to 7,800. Terapia, another drugs maker in demand closed 100 lei weaker to 11,300, despite some deals struck at 11,500 during the trading session.
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks closed lower across the board on Thursday after activity slowed down ahead of the long weekend which starts with a bank holiday on Friday.
Most blue chips suffered corrections with investor interest waning. One of the most liquid shares, drug maker Pliva, traded only 376 shares this week, compared to almost 17,000 last week.
Traders blamed the fall of prices and slower trading on a lack of investors, but disagreed over whether this pointed to a downward trend or was just a temporary correction.
LJUBLJANA
The Slovenian SBI index rose 1.49 percent this week to close on Thursday at 1,600.40.

"Many brokers feel better if they sell some of their shares before leaving on holiday. Most of the volume is usually accounted for by foreigners and they do not sell, so there was not much profit-taking," said Zoran
Spasenic, a trader at brokerage BPH.
